title: Events versus public delegates (publisher-subscriber safety)
hook: An event lets a class notify listeners when something happens. Unlike a public delegate field, outsiders can only subscribe and unsubscribe — they cannot wipe the handler list or raise the event themselves.

blocks.text: An **event** is a member that wraps a delegate with restricted access. Outside the declaring type, callers may use only `+=` and `-=` to subscribe and unsubscribe. Only the publisher invokes the delegate and can assign it. The standard .NET pattern is **EventHandler** or **EventHandler<TEventArgs>** with a sender and event-args object. Multiple subscribers run **synchronously** in subscription order when the publisher raises the event.

entries.plainDefinition: A delegate-backed member that exposes add and remove accessors instead of public get/set.
The type that declares and raises the event when something happens.
Code that += a handler to react when the event fires.
The standard delegate shape: void Handler(object? sender, TEventArgs e).

blocks.text: A long-lived Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) consumer that exposes a public Action field lets any code assign null and drop production handlers — or invoke the callback whenever it wants. The **event** keyword fixes that: outsiders subscribe but never control invocation. The flip side is **memory leaks**: the publisher's invocation list holds the subscriber's delegate, which holds the subscriber instance. A scoped per-message processor that += and never -= stays rooted until the host dies.

blocks.title: Unsubscribe in finally or Dispose
blocks.body: Store the handler in a named variable, += in try, -= in finally. Unsubscribing a freshly allocated lambda with the same body does nothing — delegate identity matters, not source text.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Publisher declares event
items.body: Field-like event: public event EventHandler<T>? Name; Custom add/remove when you need locking or weak references.

items.title: Subscriber += handler
items.body: The compiler calls the add accessor. The invocation list grows.

items.title: Publisher raises
items.body: Inside the declaring type: Name?.Invoke(this, args). Handlers run left to right, synchronously.

items.title: Subscriber -= handler
items.body: Must pass the same delegate instance that was added. Dispose or finally blocks prevent leaks.

blocks.title: Using a public delegate field as an event
blocks.body: public Action<T>? OnDone lets callers invoke or null the field. Use event Action<T>? Done instead.

blocks.title: Raising from a background thread without documenting reentrancy
blocks.body: Handlers run on the raiser's thread. UI subscribers may need BeginInvoke or a synchronization context — document threading expectations.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: when an SQS consumer stops processing after a metrics handler throws, the invocation list aborted mid-raise — add per-handler try/catch via GetInvocationList and log which handler index failed. Memory leaks from events show in dotnet-gcdump as hosted services holding scoped processor graphs — search for EventHandler delegates rooted from a singleton host. Thread-pool queue depth spikes when a slow synchronous handler blocks the raise thread during DrainAsync.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying events are thread-safe for concurrent += during raise without custom locking. Not knowing multicast exception semantics — one throw skips remaining handlers. Using public Action<T>? instead of event and calling it 'the same thing'. Unsubscribing with a new lambda and wondering why the leak persists.

interviewTakeaways: event exposes only += and -= outside the type; only the publisher invokes and assigns the backing delegate.
Multicast raises run synchronously; one handler exception aborts the rest unless you iterate GetInvocationList.
In production, scoped subscribers on singleton hosts leak until -= in Dispose — verify with a heap dump under load.
60s: event protects the invocation list from outsiders. Raise synchronously left-to-right. Exception skips later handlers. GetInvocationList isolates faults. Same delegate instance for -=.
Follow-up: when would you replace C# events with System.Threading.Channels?
commonPitfalls: Saying events are automatically thread-safe gets you rejected — concurrent += during raise needs custom add/remove locking.
Unsubscribing with a newly allocated lambda — delegate identity matters, not source text equality.
Strong answer: 'event for subscribe-only API. Snapshot and GetInvocationList when metrics can throw but routing must continue. Always -= in Dispose on long-lived publishers.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Browser events require the same function reference to remove, exactly like C# -=. JavaScript does not stop you from replacing onclick entirely; C# event does.
addEventListener/removeEventListener is subscribe/unsubscribe. C# events hide the delegate invocation list from outside callers.
